1. PREMISE: Your framing treats this as a problem of attention—a deficit in focusing capacity that needs correction through effort or technique. This rests on a false assumption: that the forward-looking pattern is primarily a failure of perception rather than a learned protective mechanism with genuine payoffs you have not yet renounced. The entire analysis turns on recognizing that you are not failing to focus; you are successfully using anticipation as a tool to manage discomfort, and no attention technique will displace it until you name what discomfort it serves and decide the cost of that protection exceeds its benefit.

2. STAKES: Your family members are losing your actual presence during their finite time in your life—they are not recovering those conversations, observations, or shared moments of full attention. You are losing irreplaceable memory formation and relational depth; once a semester ends, the opportunity to inhabit it fully does not return. Your future self will inherit the consequences of this pattern: a history of major life periods experienced as transitions rather than substance, and the compounded skill deficit of having avoided practicing presence during the years when you had fewest competing demands. Your institution (school) is losing the intellectual engagement that converts coursework from credential-acquisition into genuine learning; the resources you mention are rendering diminishing returns because they are not being metabolically used. The immediate discomfort you are avoiding through forward-focus is also losing: you never develop tolerance for it, frustration, or the texture of difficult work, which means it will remain a destabilizing force in your later career and relationships.

3. DIRECTIVE: Do not permit yourself to generate or entertain anticipatory thoughts about the next bounded period (internship, family event, semester, assignment, break) until the current one has concluded. The decisive reason is that you cannot simultaneously practice presence and maintain an escape route; the protective mechanism only loses its grip when you remove the permission to use it. [Alternative: Allow yourself to anticipate the next period while attempting to focus more intently on the current one. This produces the illusion of progress while maintaining your existing protective apparatus intact; the primary risk is that the discomfort driving the pattern intensifies silently at high probability, causing you to retreat further into forward-focus.]

4. RECOMMENDATION: Establish a rule forbidding yourself to name, reference, or imagine what comes after the present semester, assignment, gathering, or interval until that interval has formally terminated. The alternative generates a worse outcome because it treats anticipation as compatible with presence, when the two are neurologically antagonistic—you cannot genuinely direct attention backward while your mind is structured to escape forward. One legitimate objection exists: that some planning (course registration, logistics) requires looking ahead, and this directive appears to prohibit it. The specific reason this objection does not outweigh the directive is that planning and daydreaming are distinct; you can execute logistical thinking in bounded, instrumental windows (one hour per month for registration decisions) without converting your baseline orientation into permanent future-scanning. The cost of this discipline is high: you will feel the full weight of assignments you dislike, family gatherings that are unstructured or boring, and stretches of ordinary time without the numbing effect of forward-focus. That weight is the point; it is the signal that presence is occurring. Therefore: Cease constructing escape narratives through anticipation, and allow each bounded interval to conclude before permitting your attention to migrate toward what follows.
